claim: RBM15 is methylated by protein arginine methyltransferase 1 (PRMT1) at residue R578.
source: We demonstrate that RBM15 is methylated by protein arginine methyltransferase 1 (PRMT1) at residue R578, leading to its degradation via ubiquitylation by an E3 ligase (CNOT4).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis identifying the methylation site and in vitro/in vivo methylation assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: Methylation of RBM15 at R578 leads to its degradation via ubiquitylation by CNOT4.
source: We demonstrate that RBM15 is methylated by protein arginine methyltransferase 1 (PRMT1) at residue R578, leading to its degradation via ubiquitylation by an E3 ligase (CNOT4).
evidence: Demonstrated through ubiquitylation assays in Figure 3 showing CNOT4-mediated ubiquitylation of methylated RBM15 and protein stability experiments in Figure 2.

claim: Overexpression of PRMT1 in acute megakaryocytic leukemia cell lines blocks megakaryocyte terminal differentiation by downregulation of RBM15 protein level.
source: Overexpression of PRMT1 in acute megakaryocytic leukemia cell lines blocks megakaryocyte terminal differentiation by downregulation of RBM15 protein level.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4E where PRMT1 V2 overexpression in CD34+ cells blocked MK maturation.

claim: Restoring RBM15 protein level rescues megakaryocyte terminal differentiation blocked by PRMT1 overexpression.
source: Restoring RBM15 protein level rescues megakaryocyte terminal differentiation blocked by PRMT1 overexpression.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 4H showing that overexpression of RBM15 or R578K rescued MK differentiation in CD34+ cells expressing PRMT1 V2.

claim: RBM15 binds to pre-messenger RNA intronic regions of genes important for megakaryopoiesis such as GATA1, RUNX1, TAL1 and c-MPL.
source: At the molecular level, RBM15 binds to pre-messenger RNA intronic regions of genes important for megakaryopoiesis such as GATA1, RUNX1, TAL1 and c-MPL.
evidence: Supported by RIP-seq data shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures showing RBM15 binding peaks on these genes.

claim: RBM15 binding to specific intronic regions recruits the splicing factor SF3B1 to the same sites for alternative splicing.
source: Furthermore, preferential binding of RBM15 to specific intronic regions recruits the splicing factor SF3B1 to the same sites for alternative splicing.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 7 showing co-immunoprecipitation of RBM15 with SF3B1 and RIP assays showing SF3B1 binding to the same regions as RBM15 on GATA1 and c-MPL pre-mRNA.

claim: PRMT1 regulates alternative RNA splicing via reducing RBM15 protein concentration.
source: Therefore, PRMT1 regulates alternative RNA splicing via reducing RBM15 protein concentration.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6 showing changes in alternative splicing ratios of GATA1, RUNX1, and c-MPL when RBM15 or PRMT1 levels are manipulated.

claim: PRMT1 expression is higher in AMKL patient samples than in other types of acute myeloid leukemia.
source: Gene expression data from AMKL patient samples (Bourquin et al., 2006) shows a higher PRMT1 expression level than other types of acute myeloid leukemia.
evidence: Based on analysis of microarray data set GSE4119 shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: High expression of PRMT1 is correlated with poor survival rate in acute myeloid leukemia.
source: Furthermore, high expression of PRMT1 is correlated with poor survival rate in acute myeloid leukemia (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in survival analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B using TCGA data.

claim: RBM15 is methylated at R578 by mass spectrometry analysis.
source: We found that RBM15 is methylated at R578 by mass spectrometry analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Direct identification by tandem mass spectrometry shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The methylation site R578 on RBM15 is conserved across diverse species.
source: Alignment of the RBM15 sequences covering the methylation site shows that the methylation site is conserved across diverse species (Figure 1A)
evidence: Shown by sequence alignment in Figure 1A including human, dog, pig, mouse, rat, horse, chicken, zebrafish, and frog.

claim: The methylation site R578 is downstream of the RBM15 RNA binding domains.
source: Alignment of the RBM15 sequences covering the methylation site shows that the methylation site is conserved across diverse species (Figure 1A) and downstream of the RBM15 RNA binding domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Shown in schematic diagram in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Affinity purified Flag-tagged RBM15 protein is more efficiently methylated than the R578K mutant in western blots in transfected 293T cells.
source: We observed that affinity purified Flag-tagged RBM15 protein is more efficiently methylated than the R578K mutant in western blots (WBs) in transfected 293T cells (Figure 1B, compare lanes 1 and 2)
evidence: Shown by western blot with anti-monomethyl arginine antibody in Figure 1B.

claim: Overexpressing either PRMT1 V1 or V2 isoform enhanced the mono-methylation of RBM15.
source: Overexpressing either isoform enhanced the mono-methylation of RBM15 (Figure 1C, compare lanes 1, 2 and 3)
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot in Figure 1C showing increased mono-methylation with both V1 and V2 overexpression.

claim: PRMT1 V2 dimethylated RBM15 more effectively than the V1 isoform.
source: Overexpressing either isoform enhanced the mono-methylation of RBM15 (Figure 1C, compare lanes 1, 2 and 3) and the V2 dimethylated RBM15 more effectively than the V1.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1C by western blot with dimethyl arginine antibody.

claim: PRMT1 V2 contains additional amino acids in the N terminal region relative to V1.
source: Given that the V2 contains additional amino acids in the N terminal region relative to V1 (Figure 1D), it is striking that the PRMT1 V2 is primarily responsible for the dimethylation of RBM15 in vivo (Figure 1C).
evidence: Shown in sequence comparison in Figure 1D.

claim: PRMT1 V2 is primarily responsible for the dimethylation of RBM15 in vivo.
source: Given that the V2 contains additional amino acids in the N terminal region relative to V1 (Figure 1D), it is striking that the PRMT1 V2 is primarily responsible for the dimethylation of RBM15 in vivo (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing V1 and V2 effects on RBM15 dimethylation in Figure 1C.

claim: The RBM15 peptide was dimethylated as efficiently as the histone H4 peptide in vitro without monomethylated peptides detected.
source: In vitro methylation assays showed that the RBM15 peptide was dimethylated as efficiently as the histone H4 peptide without monomethylated peptides detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: Shown by in vitro methylation assay in Figure 1—figure supplement 3G.

claim: Only the WT RBM15 protein but not the R578K mutant was effectively dimethylated by PRMT1 in vitro.
source: We then used purified Flag-RBM15 from 293T cells to conduct in vitro methylation assays. Only the WT RBM15 protein but not the R578K mutant was effectively dimethylated by PRMT1 in vitro (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro methylation assay shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mono-methylated RBM15 is a transient intermediate in vivo.
source: These results together with in vivo methylation data collectively argue that mono-methylated RBM15 is a transient intermediate in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that dimethylation is the predominant form detected and monomethylation is not detected in peptide assays.

claim: Reducing the expression of PRMT1 decreased the methylation level of the endogenous RBM15.
source: To confirm that PRMT1 is responsible for in vivo methylation, we made MEG-01 stable cell lines expressing doxycycline-inducible shRNA against PRMT1. We detected the methylated form of RBM15 with both mono-methyl and dimethyl antibodies. Reducing the expression of PRMT1 decreased the methylation level of the endogenous RBM15 (Figure 1F).
evidence: Shown by immunoprecipitation and western blot in Figure 1F.

claim: Treatment with DB75 (a PRMT1 inhibitor) reduced RBM15 methylation in leukemia cells.
source: When the leukemia cells were treated with DB75 (a PRMT1 inhibitor) (Yan et al., 2014), RBM15 methylation was reduced (Figure 1G).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot in Figure 1G showing reduced methylation after DB75 treatment.

claim: PRMT1 enzymatic activity is responsible for the methylation of RBM15 at R578.
source: Therefore, we concluded that PRMT1 enzymatic activity is responsible for the methylation of RBM15 at R578.
evidence: Concluded from PRMT1 knockdown and inhibitor experiments showing reduced RBM15 methylation.

claim: RBM15 might be methylated by other PRMTs and at other sites since some methylation signals are present despite PRMT1 knock-down or inhibition and in the R578K mutant.
source: RBM15 might be methylated by other PRMTs and at other sites since some methylation signals, especially the monomethylation signals, are present despite PRMT1 knock-down or inhibition and in the R578K mutant.
evidence: Inferred from residual methylation signals observed in PRMT1 knockdown and R578K mutant experiments.

claim: The PRMT1-dependent R578 methylation forms the majority of dimethylated species.
source: Nevertheless, the PRMT1-dependent R578 methylation forms the majority of dimethylated species.
evidence: Concluded from the substantial reduction in dimethylation upon PRMT1 knockdown or inhibition.

claim: When RBM15 was co-expressed together with PRMT1, RBM15 protein level was reduced.
source: When RBM15 was co-expressed together with PRMT1, RBM15 protein level was reduced.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2A where PRMT1 overexpression reduced RBM15 protein levels.

claim: The PRMT1 V2 isoform caused a greater reduction of RBM15 protein level than V1.
source: Strikingly, the V2 isoform (detected by V2-specific antibody) caused a greater reduction of RBM15 protein level (Figure 2A), which coincided with the PRMT1 V2's capability for RBM15 dimethylation (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot in Figure 2A comparing V1 and V2 effects on RBM15 protein levels.

claim: Treatment with non-specific methyltransferase inhibitors (adox + MTA) increased RBM15 protein levels in MEG-01 cells.
source: To further confirm that methylation triggers protein degradation, we used non-specific methyltransferase inhibitors (adenosine dialdehyde [adox] + methylthioadenosine [MTA]) (Figure 2B, left panel) as well as DB75 (Figure 2B right panel) to treat MEG-01 cells.
evidence: Shown by western blot in Figure 2B demonstrating increased RBM15 protein after inhibitor treatment.

claim: PRMT1 knockdown increased RBM15 protein level but not the RBM15 mRNA level in MEG-01 cells.
source: Consistently, PRMT1 knockdown increased RBM15 protein level (Figure 2C, left panel) but not the RBM15 mRNA level (Figure 2C, right panel) in MEG-01 cells as well as in other leukemia cells (data not shown).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot and real-time PCR in Figure 2C.

claim: Overexpression of PRMT1 V2 reduced RBM15 protein level without changing RBM15 mRNA levels.
source: Conversely, overexpression of PRMT1 V2 (Figure 2D, left panel) reduced RBM15 protein level. Given that the RBM15 mRNA levels in PRMT1 knockdown cells and in PRMT1 overexpressing cells were the same as in the control MEG-01 cells (Figure 2D middle and right panels), we concluded that PRMT1 controls RBM15 at protein level.
evidence: Shown by western blot and real-time PCR in Figure 2D.

claim: PRMT1 controls RBM15 at protein level.
source: Given that the RBM15 mRNA levels in PRMT1 knockdown cells and in PRMT1 overexpressing cells were the same as in the control MEG-01 cells (Figure 2D middle and right panels), we concluded that PRMT1 controls RBM15 at protein level.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing protein level changes without mRNA level changes.

claim: Specific knockdown of PRMT1 V2 resulted in higher RBM15 protein level.
source: Finally, we observed that the specific knockdown of PRMT1 V2 resulted in higher RBM15 protein level (Figure 2E).
evidence: Shown by western blot in Figure 2E using V2-specific shRNA.

claim: The PRMT1 V2 enzymatic activity plays a major role in regulating the stability of the RBM15 protein.
source: Taken together, we concluded that the PRMT1 V2 enzymatic activity plays a major role in regulating the stability of the RBM15 protein.
evidence: Concluded from multiple experiments showing V2-specific effects on RBM15 protein stability.

claim: The RBM15 R578K mutant protein remained stable regardless of overexpression of PRMT1 V2.
source: When we co-expressed RBM15 R578K together with PRMT1 V2 protein in 293T cells, we found that the mutant protein remained stable regardless of overexpression of PRMT1 V2 (Figure 2F, compare lanes 4 and 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot in Figure 2F showing stable R578K protein levels with PRMT1 V2 overexpression.

claim: Methylation of RBM15 at R578 is the direct cause for protein degradation.
source: Thus, methylation of RBM15 at R578 is the direct cause for protein degradation.
evidence: Concluded from the observation that the R578K mutant is resistant to PRMT1-mediated degradation.

claim: The Flag-tagged RBM15 mutant has longer half-life compared with the WT RBM15.
source: To further determine whether RBM15 degradation is affected by methylation on R578, we compared the half-life of the WT versus the mutant RBM15 proteins. The Flag-tagged RBM15 mutant has longer half-life compared with the WT RBM15 (Figure 2G).
evidence: Demonstrated by cycloheximide chase assay in Figure 2G.

claim: The Flag tag does not affect RBM15 protein stability as the tagged RBM15 and endogenous RBM15 have similar half-life.
source: Tag does not affect protein stability as the tagged RBM15 and endogenous RBM15 have similar half-life.
evidence: Stated based on comparison of half-life experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The proteasome inhibitor MG132 stabilized the RBM15 protein.
source: We showed that the proteasome inhibitor MG132 stabilized the RBM15 protein, which indicates that the degradation is mediated by ubiquitylation (Figure 3A).
evidence: Shown by western blot in Figure 3A demonstrating increased RBM15 protein after MG132 treatment.

claim: RBM15 degradation is mediated by ubiquitylation.
source: We showed that the proteasome inhibitor MG132 stabilized the RBM15 protein, which indicates that the degradation is mediated by ubiquitylation (Figure 3A).
evidence: Inferred from the stabilization of RBM15 by proteasome inhibitor MG132.

claim: RBM15 protein is ubiquitylated as shown by nickel bead purification under denaturing conditions.
source: To further confirm that the RBM15 protein is ubiquitylated, we used nickel beads to purify the poly-ubiquitylated form of RBM15 under denaturing conditions from 293T cells expressing the poly-histidine-tagged ubiquitin and Flag-tagged RBM15 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by nickel bead pull-down and western blot in Figure 3B.

claim: Significantly less R578K RBM15 protein was modified by ubiquitin compared with the WT RBM15 protein.
source: To investigate whether methylation of RBM15 by PRMT1 is required for RBM15 ubiquitylation, we mutated the methylation site to lysine. Compared with the WT RBM15 protein, significantly less R578K RBM15 protein was modified by ubiquitin (Figure 3C compare lanes 4 and 5,) when the respective plasmids were co-expressed in 293T cells.
evidence: Shown by immunoprecipitation and western blot in Figure 3C.

claim: Methylation on R578 for protein ubiquitylation is one major pathway for RBM15 degradation.
source: Thus, methylation on R578 for protein ubiquitylation is one major pathway for RBM15 degradation.
evidence: Concluded from the reduced ubiquitylation of R578K mutant compared to wild-type RBM15.

claim: After DB75 treatment, less ubiquitylated RBM15 proteins were observed in endogenous RBM15.
source: To validate that endogenous RBM15 is also ubiquitylated in a methylation-dependent manner, we treated the MEG-01 cells with PRMT1 inhibitor DB75. After DB75 treatment, less ubiquitylated RBM15 proteins were observed (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and western blot in Figure 3D.

claim: PRMT1 physically interacts with the CCR4-NOT complex via the CAF1 (aka CNOT7) subunit for RNA export.
source: PRMT1 has been shown to physically interact with the CCR4-NOT complex via the CAF1 (aka CNOT7) subunit for RNA export (Kerr et al., 2011; Robin-Lespinasse et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: CNOT4, a subunit of the CCR4-NOT complex, has been shown to be an E3 ligase.
source: Furthermore, CNOT4, a subunit of the CCR4-NOT complex, has been shown to be an E3 ligase (Albert et al., 2002).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: When RBM15 was co-expressed with PRMT1 and CNOT4, RBM15 was more severely ubiquitylated than RBM15 expressed with PRMT1 or CNOT4 alone.
source: To examine whether CNOT4 might be responsible for ubiquitylation of RBM15, we co-expressed CNOT4 with RBM15 in 293T cells. Strikingly, when RBM15 was co-expressed with PRMT1 and CNOT4, RBM15 was more severely ubiquitylated than RBM15 expressed with PRMT1 or CNOT4 alone (Figure 3E).
evidence: Shown by immunoprecipitation and western blot in Figure 3E.

claim: PRMT1 interacts with RBM15 WT and mutant proteins in 293T cells.
source: We also detected the interaction between PRMT1 and RBM15 WT and mutant proteins in 293T cells (Figure 3E lanes 3,4 and 7,8).
evidence: Shown by co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 3E.

claim: Only the WT and not the mutant RBM15 interacted with HA-tagged CNOT4.
source: Moreover, only the WT and not the mutant RBM15 interacted with HA-tagged CNOT4 (Figure 3E lane 3, 4).
evidence: Shown by co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 3E.

claim: The RBM15 R578K mutant had significantly less ubiquitylated RBM15 protein, suggesting that methylation is required for subsequent ubiquitylation by the CNOT4 complex.
source: In Figure 3E and Figure 3C, we showed that the RBM15 R578K, which cannot be methylated by PRMT1, had significantly less ubiquitylated RBM15 protein. This data strongly suggest that methylation is required for subsequent ubiquitylation by the CNOT4 complex.
evidence: Concluded from comparison of ubiquitylation levels between WT and R578K mutant in Figures 3C and 3E.

claim: CNOT4 knockdown increased the amount of endogenous RBM15 protein in MEG-01 cells.
source: To further confirm that CNOT4 is the enzyme responsible for endogenous RBM15 ubiquitylation, we showed that CNOT4 knockdown (WB in Figure 3F and real-time polychromase chain reaction [PCR] in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) increased the amount of endogenous RBM15 protein in MEG-01 cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot in Figure 3F and PCR in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: When MEG-01 cells were treated with DB75, CNOT4 knockdown did not further stabilize the RBM15 protein.
source: When MEG-01 cells were treated with DB75, CNOT4 knockdown did not further stabilize the RBM15 protein (Figure 3F).
evidence: Shown by western blot in Figure 3F demonstrating no additive effect of DB75 and CNOT4 knockdown.

claim: Methylation is required for the subsequent degradation of the RBM15 protein.
source: These results confirm that methylation is required for the subsequent degradation of the RBM15 protein.
evidence: Concluded from the observation that CNOT4 knockdown and PRMT1 inhibition do not have additive effects.

claim: Removal of one allele of CNOT4 stabilized the endogenous RBM15 protein levels.
source: We used the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR) technology to knockout one allele of CNOT4 gene in 293T cells. We also found that removal of one allele of CNOT4 stabilized the endogenous RBM15 protein levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B&C).
evidence: Demonstrated by CRISPR knockout and western blot in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B&C.

claim: The methylated RBM15 protein was more efficiently ubiquitylated by CNOT4 than the purified RBM15 R578K in vitro.
source: We then purified the RBM15 and CNOT4 proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) to do in vitro ubiquitylaton assay. The methylated RBM15 protein (Flag-tagged) by PRMT1 was more efficiently ubiquitylated by CNOT4 than the purified RBM15 R578 in vitro (Figure 3G compare lane 5 to lane 3).
evidence: Shown by in vitro ubiquitylation assay in Figure 3G.

claim: CNOT4 is an E3 ligase responsible for degrading the methylated RBM15.
source: Taken together, we demonstrated that the RBM15 protein stability is negatively regulated by PRMT1-mediated methylation at R578, and CNOT4 is an E3 ligase responsible for degrading the methylated RBM15.
evidence: Concluded from multiple experiments showing CNOT4-dependent ubiquitylation and degradation of methylated RBM15.

claim: The di-methylated peptide bound specifically to the CNOT4 protein.
source: To understand further whether the methylation site on RBM15 is sufficient to bind to CNOT4 complex, we synthesized two RBM15 peptides covering the arginine methylation sites to pull-down CNOT4 from cell extract. The di-methylated peptide bound specifically to the CNOT4 protein (Figure 3H)
evidence: Demonstrated by peptide pull-down assay in Figure 3H.

claim: Either CNOT4 or subunits in the CNOT4 complex directly interacts with RBM15 via the methylation mark.
source: This result implies that either CNOT4 or subunits in the CNOT4 complex directly interacts with RBM15 via the methylation mark.
evidence: Inferred from the specific binding of methylated peptide to CNOT4 in pull-down assays.

claim: PRMT1 expression level was the lowest in LT-HSC and higher especially in myeloid progenitor cells.
source: PRMT1 RNA levels were measured in isolated mouse long-term hematopoietic stem cells (LT-HSC), short-term hematopoietic stem cells (ST-HSC), progenitor cells and terminally differentiated lineages. PRMT1 expression level was the lowest in LT-HSC and higher especially in myeloid progenitor cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Shown by real-time PCR in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: Megakaryocyte-erythrocyte progenitor (MEP) cells expressed the highest level of PRMT1.
source: Megakaryocyte-–erythrocyte progenitor (MEP) cells expressed the highest level of PRMT1.
evidence: Stated based on real-time PCR data from mouse hematopoietic lineages.

claim: The expression profiles of PRMT1 and RBM15 in different lineages are shared between humans and mice.
source: We also checked the expression of PRMT1 and RBM15 in human cells with HemaExplorer (Bagger et al., 2013). The expression profiles of PRMT1 and RBM15 in different lineages are shared between humans and mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: Based on analysis of HemaExplorer database shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-G.

claim: The mRNA level of RBM15 does not change as dramatically as that of PRMT1 among different lineages.
source: The mRNA level of RBM15 does not change as dramatically as that of PRMT1 among different lineages, which implies that post-transcriptional modification such as arginine methylation of RBM15 might contribute to the regulation of RBM15 protein levels.
evidence: Observed from expression data in different hematopoietic lineages.

claim: Upon PMA stimulation, upregulation of the RBM15 protein within 12 hr and simultaneous down-regulation of the PRMT1 V2 protein were observed.
source: To understand the biological functions of PRMT1 in MK differentiation, we used phorbol myristate acetate (PMA) to stimulate MEG-01 cells into mature MK cells (Ogura et al., 1988). Upon PMA stimulation, we observed upregulation of the RBM15 protein within 12 hr and simultaneous down-regulation of the PRMT1 V2 protein (Figure 4A left and middle panels).
evidence: Shown by western blot time course in Figure 4A.

claim: During PMA stimulation, neither the RBM15 mRNA level nor the total PRMT1 protein level changed more than 1.5-folds.
source: During the incubation period, neither the RBM15 mRNA level (Figure 4A, right panel) nor the total PRMT1 protein level (mainly V1 isoform) changed more than 1.5-folds, nevertheless we found that RBM15 protein level was significantly increased.
evidence: Shown by real-time PCR and western blot in Figure 4A.

claim: The isoform V2-mediated methylation is one mechanism for upregulating RBM15 protein level during MK differentiation.
source: The methyl-RBM15 level reduced coinciding with the decrease of the isoform V2 protein (detected by V2-specific antibody). Thus we conclude the isoform V2 –mediated methylation is one mechanism for upregulating RBM15 protein level, although we cannot rule out other possibilities such as enhanced protein translation.
evidence: Concluded from correlation between V2 protein decrease and RBM15 protein increase during PMA stimulation.

claim: After stimulation with PMA for 7 days, more CD41+ cells were detected in cells expressing WT and R578K RBM15.
source: To assess RBM15 effects on MK differentiation, we ectopically expressed the WT and the R578K mutant proteins in MEG-01 cells by retroviruses. After stimulation with PMA for 7 days, more CD41+ cells (Figure 4B) as well as higher levels of polyploidy (Figure 4C) were detected.
evidence: Shown by FACS analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: The RBM15 R578K generated more CD41+ cells compared to WT RBM15, which may be explained by increased RBM15 R578K stability.
source: In comparison to WT RBM15, the RBM15 R578K generated more CD41+ cells, which may be explained by increased RBM15 R578K stability (Figure 3).
evidence: Observed in FACS analysis and explained by previous stability data.

claim: DB75-treated CD34+ cells produced a higher percentage of CD61+CD42+ mature MK cells compared with the control.
source: However, the cell line differentiation system can only mimic certain aspects of normal megakaryopoiesis. For example, we cannot detect CD42 in MEG-01 cells upon PMA stimulation. Therefore, we performed MK differentiation assays with adult human CD34+ cells. Compared with the control, DB75-treated cells produced a higher percentage of CD61+CD42+ mature MK cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: Shown by FACS analysis in Figure 4D.

claim: Ectopic expression of PRMT1 V2 in CD34+ cells promoted the generation of single positive CD61+ MK progenitor cells but blocked MK cell maturation.
source: Conversely, ectopic expression of PRMT1 V2 in CD34+ cells promoted the generation of single positive CD61+ MK progenitor cells but blocked MK cell maturation (Figure 4E).
evidence: Shown by FACS analysis in Figure 4E.

claim: Knockdown of RBM15 by shRNAs blocked MK maturation.
source: Like PRMT1 overexpression, knockdown of RBM15 by shRNAs blocked MK maturation (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Shown by FACS analysis in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overexpression of both RBM15 and its mutant promoted the maturation of CD34+ cells.
source: and overexpression of both RBM15 and its mutant promoted the maturation of CD34+ cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: Shown by FACS analysis in Figure 4G.

claim: Overexpression of RBM15 or RBM15 R578K rescued MK differentiation in CD34+ cells expressing PRMT1 V2.
source: Overexpression of RBM15 or RBM15 R578K rescued MK differentiation in CD34+ cells expressing PRMT1 V2 (Figure 4H).
evidence: Shown by FACS analysis in Figure 4H.

claim: PRMT1 controls megakaryopoiesis via controlling RBM15 protein levels.
source: Taken together, PRMT1 controls megakaryopoiesis via controlling RBM15 protein levels.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing that manipulating PRMT1 and RBM15 levels affects MK differentiation.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis showed that RBM15 was associated with ASH2 and WTAP, two known RBM15-bound proteins.
source: To understand how RBM15 protein level controls megakaryocytic differentiation, we affinity purified RBM15-associated proteins from 293T cells, which express endogenous RBM15 protein. Mass spectrometry analysis showed that RBM15 was associated with ASH2 and WTAP, two known RBM15-bound proteins (Horiuchi et al., 2013; Lee and Skalnik, 2012) as well as proteins involved in RNA splicing (Figure 7—source data 1)
evidence: Based on mass spectrometry analysis of RBM15-associated proteins.

claim: RBM15 resides in nuclear splicing speckles by confocal microscopy.
source: which is consistent with prior findings that RBM15 resides in nuclear splicing speckles (Horiuchi et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: RBM15 binds to RUNX1, GATA1 and c-MPL mRNAs but not to control GAPDH mRNA.
source: Thus, we reasoned that RBM15 might regulate alternative splicing. We performed RNA immunoprecipitation assay (RIP) under stringent wash conditions with an RBM15 antibody recognizing the N-terminal region, followed by real-time polychromase chain reaction (RT-PCR) to detect genes known to be important for MK differentiation. We detected the bindings of RUNX1, GATA1 and c-MPL mRNAs with RBM15, while we did not detect that of control GAPDH mRNA (Figure 5A).
evidence: Shown by RIP followed by real-time PCR in Figure 5A.

claim: 1297 genes were identified to which RBM15 binds directly by RIP-seq.
source: Then we took an unbiased approach to identify global RBM15 target genes using RIP-seq. We have identified 1297 genes to which RBM15 binds directly (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Based on RIP-seq analysis.

claim: Fifty-five percent of RBM15 binding sites are in intronic regions and 41% are in 3'UTR regions.
source: Fifty-five percent of RBM15 binding sites are in intronic regions and 41% are in 3'UTR regions, with the remainder in 5'UTRs and CDS elements (Figure 5B).
evidence: Shown by distribution analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: Gene ontology pathway analysis showed RBM15 regulates genes involved in differentiation and signal transduction via binding to intronic regions.
source: Gene ontology (GO) pathway analysis showed RBM15 regulates genes involved in differentiation and signal transduction via binding to intronic regions, whereas genes involved in RNA splicing and metabolic pathways were regulated via binding to 3'UTRs (Figure 5C&D).
evidence: Based on GO pathway analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Genes involved in RNA splicing and metabolic pathways were regulated via RBM15 binding to 3'UTRs.
source: Gene ontology (GO) pathway analysis showed RBM15 regulates genes involved in differentiation and signal transduction via binding to intronic regions, whereas genes involved in RNA splicing and metabolic pathways were regulated via binding to 3'UTRs (Figure 5C&D).
evidence: Based on GO pathway analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Among the RBM15 targeting genes with binding sites in introns are transcription factors RUNX1, GATA1, and TAL1.
source: We found that overexpression of PRMT1 V1 and V2 isoforms as well as reducing the expression level of RBM15 enhanced mitochondria biogenesis in MEG-01 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), which implies that PRMT1-RBM15 axis regulates metabolism. Among the RBM15 targeting genes with binding sites in introns are transcription factors known to be important for MK differentiation: RUNX1, GATA1, and TAL1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1,2).
evidence: Shown by RIP-seq data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1,2.

claim: Overexpression of PRMT1 V1 and V2 isoforms as well as reducing the expression level of RBM15 enhanced mitochondria biogenesis in MEG-01 cells.
source: We found that overexpression of PRMT1 V1 and V2 isoforms as well as reducing the expression level of RBM15 enhanced mitochondria biogenesis in MEG-01 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), which implies that PRMT1-RBM15 axis regulates metabolism.
evidence: Shown by mitotracker staining in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: PRMT1-RBM15 axis regulates metabolism.
source: We found that overexpression of PRMT1 V1 and V2 isoforms as well as reducing the expression level of RBM15 enhanced mitochondria biogenesis in MEG-01 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), which implies that PRMT1-RBM15 axis regulates metabolism.
evidence: Inferred from the effect on mitochondria biogenesis and GO pathway analysis showing metabolic genes as targets.

claim: LEF1 has been shown to interact with RUNX1 genetically and biochemically.
source: Although the transcription factor LEF1 has not yet been linked to MK differentiation, LEF1 has been shown to interact with RUNX1 genetically and biochemically (Daga et al., 1996; Mayall et al., 1997; McNerney et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: RBM15 binding peaks on c-MPL pre-mRNA in the RIP-seq data.
source: RBM15 binding peaks on c-MPL pre-mRNA in the RIP-seq data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown in RIP-seq data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: DEXSeq detected 9704 differential exon usage events with P value lower than 0.05 and fold change higher than 1.2 fold.
source: We then used two programs (DEXSeq and MISO) to detect the alterations of exon usage. DEXSeq detected 9704 differential exon usage events with P value lower than 0.05 and fold change higher than 1.2 fold.
evidence: Based on DEXSeq analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The MISO program detected 2027 differential exon usage events with Bayes factor higher than 2.
source: The MISO program detected 2027 differential exon usage events with Bayes factor higher than 2.
evidence: Based on MISO analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: RBM15 regulates differential exon usage in all eight categories in either directions.
source: RBM15 regulates differential exon usage in all eight categories in either directions (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: Shown by analysis of alternative splicing events in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Significant exon usage changes of 156 genes in the RIP-seq group were detected by both DEXSeq and MISO programs.
source: Significant exon usage changes of 156 genes in the RIP-seq group were detected by both programs (Figure 5—source data 3) including transcription factors RUNX1, GATA1, STAT5A, TAF9, TAL1, LEF1 and ZNF160 as well as chromatin remodeling factors such as macroH2A, DEK, BRD9, TLE3, NCOR1 and HDAC4.

claim: RUNX1, GATA1, STAT5A and TAL1(SCL) are well-studied transcription factors for their roles in MK differentiation.
source: RUNX1, GATA1, STAT5A and TAL1(SCL) are well-studied transcription factors for their roles in MK differentiation (Crispino, 2005; Olthof et al., 2008; Tijssen et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: Signal transduction genes important for hematopoiesis such as RPTOR and CDC42 were found on the list of RBM15 targets.
source: Signal transduction genes important for hematopoiesis such as RPTOR and CDC42 (Kaushansky and Kaushansky, 2014) were found on the list as well.
evidence: Based on RIP-seq and RNA-seq analysis.

claim: RBM15 protein level may affect hematopoiesis via multiple pathways.
source: Therefore, RBM15 protein level may affect hematopoiesis via multiple pathways.
evidence: Concluded from the diverse set of genes regulated by RBM15 including transcription factors, chromatin remodelers, and signaling molecules.

claim: RBM15 affects alternative RNA splicing of RUNX1, GATA1, TAL1, STAT5A, LEF1.
source: At a molecular level, RBM15 not only affects alternative RNA splicing such as RUNX1, GATA1, TAL1, STAT5A, LEF1 but also affects UTR utilization (e.g. TAL1), mixed exon usage (e.g. CDC42) and intron retention (e.g. macroH2A) (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Shown by MISO and DEXSeq analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: RBM15 affects UTR utilization (e.g. TAL1), mixed exon usage (e.g. CDC42) and intron retention (e.g. macroH2A).
source: At a molecular level, RBM15 not only affects alternative RNA splicing such as RUNX1, GATA1, TAL1, STAT5A, LEF1 but also affects UTR utilization (e.g. TAL1), mixed exon usage (e.g. CDC42) and intron retention (e.g. macroH2A) (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Shown by MISO and DEXSeq analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: After knocking down RBM15, skipping of exon 2 on GATA1 was found.
source: The MISO program was used to analyze how GATA1 is alternatively spliced. After knocking down RBM15, we found skipping of exon 2 on GATA1 (Figure 5G) and validated our results by resolving GATA1 isoforms in an agarose gel (Figure 5H).
evidence: Shown by MISO analysis in Figure 5G and PCR validation in Figure 5H.

claim: GATA1 has two different isoforms: full-length GATA1 (GATA1fl), and short-form GATA1 (GATA1s), which is generated by skipping the exon 2.
source: GATA1 has two different isoforms: full-length GATA1 (GATA1fl), and short-form GATA1 (GATA1s), which is generated by skipping the exon 2 (Rainis et al., 2003).
evidence: Based on cited literature and confirmed by experimental data.

claim: In Down syndrome leukemia, GATA1fl mRNA translates the GATA1s protein when mutations on GATA1fl mRNA create an alternative translation start site.
source: In Down syndrome leukemia, GATA1fl mRNA translates the GATA1s protein when mutations on GATA1fl mRNA create an alternative translation start site.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about Down syndrome leukemia.

claim: Reducing RBM15 protein level favored the accumulation of GATA1s as the ratio of GATA1fl/GATA1s was reduced.
source: Using isoform specific probes targeting to the exon junctions of GATA1s and GATA1fl to perform real-time PCR assays, we found that reducing RBM15 protein level favored the accumulation of GATA1s as the ratio of GATA1fl/GATA1s was reduced (Figure 6A top panel).
evidence: Shown by real-time PCR with isoform-specific primers in Figure 6A.

claim: Overexpression of RBM15 reversed the ratio of GATA1fl/GATA1s in favor of GATA1fl.
source: Conversely, overexpression of RBM15 reversed the ratio of GATA1fl/GATA1s in favor of GATA1fl.
evidence: Shown by real-time PCR in Figure 6A.

claim: The RBM15 R578K protein, which is more stable, altered the ratio of GATA1fl/GATA1s more than the WT RBM15.
source: The RBM15 R578K protein, which is more stable, altered the ratio more than the WT RBM15.
evidence: Shown by real-time PCR in Figure 6A comparing WT and R578K effects.

claim: Overexpression of PRMT1 V2 in MEG-01 cells reduced the ratio of GATA1fl to GATA1s, similar to the effect of RBM15 knockdown.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of V2 in MEG-01 cells reduced the ratio of GATA1fl to GATA1s, similar to the effect of RBM15 knockdown.
evidence: Shown by real-time PCR in Figure 6A.

claim: Knockdown of PRMT1 resulted in a higher ratio of GATA1fl/GATA1s-like in cells overexpressing RBM15.
source: When we used inducible cell lines to knockdown PRMT1, we observed a higher ratio of GATA1fl/GATA1s-like in cells overexpressing RBM15 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Shown by real-time PCR in Figure 6A.

claim: All three AMKL cell lines (MEG-01, CMK, CMY) had higher GATA1fl/GATA1s ratio when treated with DB75.
source: To further probe the importance of PRMT1 enzymatic activity in alternative splicing, we used PRMT1 inhibitor DB75 to treat MEG-01 cells, CMK cells and CMY cells, which all derived from AMKL leukemia patients. All three AMKL cell lines had higher GATA1fl/GATA1s ratio when treated with DB75 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown by real-time PCR in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both isoforms of GATA1 can support MK differentiation, but only GATA1s supports unrestricted proliferation due to losing the interaction with E2F1.
source: Both isoforms of GATA1 can support MK differentiation, but only GATA1s supports unrestricted proliferation due to losing the interaction with E2F1 (Li et al., 2000).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: Fine-tuning the ratio between two different GATA1 isoforms regulates the balance between proliferation and differentiation of MK progenitors.
source: Therefore, fine-tuning the ratio between two different GATA1 isoforms regulates the balance between proliferation and differentiation of MK progenitors.
evidence: Inferred from the different functional properties of GATA1fl and GATA1s and the observed changes in their ratios.

claim: RUNX1 is required for MK differentiation as shown in a conditional RUNX1 knockout mouse model.
source: RUNX1 is required for MK differentiation as shown in a conditional RUNX1 knockout mouse model (Ichikawa et al., 2004).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: Individual RUNX1 isoforms regulate hematopoiesis differently.
source: Individual RUNX1 isoforms regulate hematopoiesis differently (Komeno et al., 2014; Tsuzuki and Seto, 2012).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: RBM15 bound to RUNX1 pre-mRNA in intronic regions and in 3'UTR.
source: RBM15 bound to RUNX1 pre-mRNA in intronic regions and in 3'UTR (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown by RIP-seq data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The MISO program found that RUNX1 is alternatively spliced by skipping exon 6, which generates RUNX1-Exon 6- protein.
source: The MISO program found that RUNX1 is alternatively spliced by skipping exon 6, which generates RUNX1-Exon 6- protein.
evidence: Based on MISO analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Overexpression of RUNX1-Exon 6- in transgenic mice leads to reduced pool of hematopoietic stem cells.
source: Overexpression of RUNX1-Exon 6- in transgenic mice leads to reduced pool of hematopoietic stem cells (Komeno et al., 2014) (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: In RBM15 knock-down MEG-01 cells, the ratio between RUNX1a and RUNX1b,c switched in favor of RUNX1a.
source: Given that RBM15 binds to the 3'UTR in exon 8 as well as to intronic regions flanking exon 7a, we investigated whether knockdown of RBM15 causes alternative 3'UTR usage to generate RUNX1a, which uses exon7a' 3'UTR. In RBM15 knock-down MEG-01 cells, the ratio between RUNX1a and RUNX1b,c switched in favor of RUNX1a.
evidence: Shown by real-time PCR in Figure 6A.

claim: RUNX1a, which lacks the transactivation domain, acts as a dominant negative regulator to antagonize the function of RUNX1b,c.
source: RUNX1a, which lacks the transactivation domain, acts as a dominant negative regulator to antagonize the function of RUNX1b,c (Ran et al., 2013a).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: Increasing the amount of RUNX1a may interfere with the differentiation into mature MKs.
source: Increasing the amount of RUNX1a may interfere with the differentiation into mature MKs.
evidence: Inferred from the dominant negative function of RUNX1a and its increased ratio upon RBM15 knockdown.

claim: Overexpression of RBM15 as well as knockdown of PRMT1 tilted the isoform balance toward RUNX1b,c.
source: Consistent with RBM15 knockdown data, we showed that overexpression of RBM15 as well as knockdown of PRMT1 tilted the isoform balance toward RUNX1b,c.
evidence: Shown by real-time PCR in Figure 6A.

claim: Overexpression of PRMT1 V2 switched the RUNX1 isoform ratio in favor of RUNX1a.
source: In agreement with the PRMT1 knockdown data, overexpression of PRMT1 V2 switched the ratio in favor of RUNX1a (Figure 6A middle panel).
evidence: Shown by real-time PCR in Figure 6A.

claim: The thrombopoietin receptor (TPOR, aka. c-MPL) is upregulated during MK differentiation.
source: The thrombopoietin receptor (TPOR, aka. c-MPL) is upregulated during MK differentiation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about MK differentiation.

claim: c-MPL has at least four described isoforms in humans.
source: c-MPL has at least four described isoforms in humans (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown in schematic in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: An additional c-MPL isoform lacking exon 9 (c-MPL-exon9-) was identified through sequencing.
source: Using reported primers (Li et al., 2000) to amplify cDNA from MEG-01 cells, we found an additional band on the PAGE gel, which was identified as an undescribed isoform lacking exon 9 (c-MPL-exon9-–) through sequencing.
evidence: Identified by PCR and sequencing shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The c-MPL-exon9– mRNA was predicted to yield a truncated protein.
source: The c-MPL-exon9– mRNA was predicted to yield a truncated protein (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The c-MPL-exon9-/c-MPL-exon9+ ratio was higher in favor of c-MPL-exon9- when RBM15 protein level is reduced.
source: Thus we designed specific primer spanning the junction between exon 8 and 10 to detect c-MPL-exon9– mRNA. We also used a pair of primers, the forward primer spanning exon 8 and 9 and the reverse primer annealing to exon 9, to detect the full-length MPL (i.e. c-MPL-exon 9+). The c-MPL-exon9-–/c-MPL-exon9+ ratio was higher in favor of c-MPL-exon9- (Figure 6A, bottom panel) when RBM15 protein level is reduced.
evidence: Shown by real-time PCR in Figure 6A.

claim: When RBM15 or RBM15 R578K was overexpressed, the c-MPL isoform ratio was down in favor of c-MPL-exon9+.
source: Furthermore, when RBM15 or RBM15 R578K was overexpressed, the ratio was down in favor of c-MPL-exon9+.
evidence: Shown by real-time PCR in Figure 6A.

claim: c-MPL exon9+ is required for MK differentiation.
source: Given that c-MPL exon9+ is required for MK differentiation, the data further support for the positive role of RBM15 at MK maturation.
evidence: Inferred from the functional requirement and the observed splicing changes.

claim: All other c-MPL isoforms with part of exon 9 or with both exon 9 and 10 missing were spliced in the same way by RBM15-PRMT1 pathway.
source: All other isoforms with part of exon 9 or with both exon 9 and 10 missing were spliced in the same way by RBM15-PRMT1 pathway (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Shown by real-time PCR in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: RBM15 enhances the inclusion of exons to produce full-length functional c-MPL like in RUNX1's case.
source: Thus, RBM15 enhances the inclusion of exons to produce full-length functional c-MPL like in RUNX1's case.
evidence: Concluded from the observed effects on exon inclusion for both c-MPL and RUNX1.

claim: Mouse Rbm15 regulates c-Mpl alternative splicing in the same fashion as human RBM15.
source: Consistent with our data, mouse Rbm15 regulates c-Mpl alternative splicing in the same fashion (Xiao et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on cited literature showing conservation of function.

claim: The GATA1fl/GATA1s ratio was increased during the course of MK differentiation in human adult CD34+ cells.
source: We monitored the isoform ratios using human adult CD34+ cells in pro-MK differentiation medium over a time course. We found that the GATA1fl/GATA1s ratio was increased, and the RUNX1a/RUNX1b,c ratio and c-MPL-exon9–/c-MPL-exon9+ ratio were decreased during the course of differentiation (Figure 6B).
evidence: Shown by time course real-time PCR in Figure 6B.

claim: The RUNX1a/RUNX1b,c ratio and c-MPL-exon9–/c-MPL-exon9+ ratio were decreased during the course of MK differentiation in human adult CD34+ cells.
source: We monitored the isoform ratios using human adult CD34+ cells in pro-MK differentiation medium over a time course. We found that the GATA1fl/GATA1s ratio was increased, and the RUNX1a/RUNX1b,c ratio and c-MPL-exon9–/c-MPL-exon9+ ratio were decreased during the course of differentiation (Figure 6B).
evidence: Shown by time course real-time PCR in Figure 6B.

claim: The isoform ratio changes in the DB75-treated CD34+ cells were the same as in the DB75-treated MEG-01 cells.
source: We observed that the isoform ratio changes in the DB75-treated CD34+ cells (Figure 6C) exactly like in the DB75-treated MEG-01 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown by comparing real-time PCR results in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: RBM15 regulates alternative RNA splicing of genes important for MK differentiation.
source: Based on these data, we concluded that RBM15 regulates alternative RNA splicing of genes important for MK differentiation.
evidence: Concluded from the observed effects on GATA1, RUNX1, and c-MPL splicing.

claim: By controlling the RBM15 protein dosage, PRMT1 thereby regulates MK differentiation.
source: By controlling the RBM15 protein dosage, PRMT1 thereby regulates MK differentiation.
evidence: Concluded from the entire set of experiments linking PRMT1-mediated RBM15 degradation to alternative splicing and MK differentiation.

claim: RBM15-associated splicing factors include SF3B1 and U2AF, known proteins in committed RNA splicing A complex that bind to branch point region.
source: To understand the detailed mechanism of how RBM15 regulates alternative splicing, we identified RBM15-associated splicing factors such as SF3B1 and U2AF, known proteins in committed RNA splicing A complex that bind to branch point region (Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Based on mass spectrometry analysis of RBM15-associated proteins.

claim: The interaction between SF3B1 and RBM15 was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation with anti-Flag antibody for Flag-tagged RBM15 proteins.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed the interaction between SF3B1 and RBM15 by co-immunoprecipitation with anti-Flag antibody for Flag-tagged RBM15 proteins (Figure 7A) and with anti-RBM15 antibody (Figure 7B).
evidence: Shown by co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: The interaction between SF3B1 and RBM15 was subject to methylation regulation.
source: To further confirm that PRMT1 enzymatic activity is important for alternative RNA splicing, we inhibited PRMT1 activity with DB75 or shPRMT1. The interaction between SF3B1 and RBM15 was subject to methylation regulation.
evidence: Shown by co-immunoprecipitation experiments with PRMT1 inhibition in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: SF3B1 was not mutated in MEG-01 cells.
source: Since SF3B1 is often mutated in leukemia cells, we sequenced the SF3B1 gene in MEG-01 cells and confirmed that SF3B1 was not mutated in this cell line.
evidence: Based on sequencing of SF3B1 gene.

claim: RBM15 was specifically associated with intronic region close to 5'end of intron 1 of GATA1.
source: From the RIP-seq data, we found that RBM15 was specifically associated with intronic region close to 5'end of intron 1 of GATA1 (Figure 7C).
evidence: Shown by RIP-seq data in Figure 7C.

claim: SF3B1 preferentially bound to the same region that RBM15 bound to on GATA1 pre-mRNA.
source: We validated the RIP-seq data by real-time PCR with primer sets covering the GATA1 intron 1. Analysis of immunoprecipitated RNA associated with SF3B1 indicated that SF3B1 also preferentially bound to the same region that RBM15 bound to.
evidence: Shown by RIP followed by real-time PCR in Figure 7D.

claim: With RBM15 knockdown, less SF3B1 was associated with GATA1 pre-mRNA.
source: Furthermore, with RBM15 knockdown, less SF3B1 was associated with GATA1 pre-mRNA (Figure 7D).
evidence: Shown by RIP followed by real-time PCR in Figure 7D.

claim: GAPDH has similar level of SF3B1 binding to introns regardless of RBM15 expression level.
source: On the other hand, GAPDH has similar level of SF3B1 binding to introns regardless of RBM15 expression level.
evidence: Shown by RIP followed by real-time PCR in Figure 7D as a negative control.

claim: RBM15 is responsible for recruiting SF3B1 to pre-mRNA molecules.
source: Thus, RBM15 is responsible for recruiting SF3B1 to pre-mRNA molecules.
evidence: Concluded from the observation that SF3B1 binding decreases when RBM15 is knocked down.

claim: For c-MPL pre-mRNA, RBM15 preferentially bound to the intron 8 and 10 with two distinct peaks.
source: For c-MPL pre-mRNA, RBM15 preferentially bound to the intron 8 and 10 of the pre-mRNA molecules with two distinct peaks (Figure 7E left)
evidence: Shown by RIP followed by real-time PCR in Figure 7E.

claim: SF3B1 bound to regions between the two RBM15 bound peaks on c-MPL pre-mRNA at higher level than other regions.
source: while SF3B1 (Figure 7E right) did bind to regions between the two RBM15 bound peaks at higher level than other regions.
evidence: Shown by RIP followed by real-time PCR in Figure 7E.

claim: When RBM15 was knocked down in MEG-01 cells, SF3B1 binding to c-MPL pre-mRNA was significantly reduced in RBM15 bound regions.
source: When we used RBM15 knockdown MEG-01 cells to do SF3B1 RIP on c-MPL pre-mRNA, we found that SF3B1 binding was significantly reduced in RBM15 bound regions (Figure 7E right).
evidence: Shown by RIP followed by real-time PCR in Figure 7E.

claim: RBM15 functions as a splicing enhancer for inclusion of exons 9 and 10 in c-MPL.
source: In this case, RBM15 functions as a splicing enhancer for inclusion of exons 9 and 10.
evidence: Concluded from the binding pattern and effects on exon inclusion.

claim: RBM15 is responsible for recruiting SF3B1 containing branch point recognition complex to introns, and methylation controls the RBM15 dosage thereby controlling alternative RNA splicing.
source: In aggregate, these data show that RBM15 is responsible for recruiting SF3B1 containing branch point recognition complex to introns, and methylation controls the RBM15 dosage thereby controlling alternative RNA splicing (Figure 7F).
evidence: Concluded from the entire set of experiments on RBM15-SF3B1 interaction and splicing regulation.

claim: PRMT1 has been previously reported to methylate arginines in PGC1-α and in RUNX1 flanked by other amino acids.
source: Although the most common sequence for arginine methylation is arginine flanked by glycines, PRMT1 has been previously reported to methylate arginines in PGC1-α and in RUNX1 flanked by other amino acids (Teyssier et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: Recent proteomics work proves that the methylation motif can be very diverse.
source: Recent proteomics work further proves that the methylation motif can be very diverse (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: Protein mono-methylation sites, in general, are redundant and prevalent and are catalyzed by multiple protein arginine methyltransferases.
source: Protein mono-methylation sites, in general, are redundant and prevalent and are catalyzed by multiple protein arginine methyltransferases (Dhar et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: It has been demonstrated that PRMT1 V1 and V2 have different substrate specificities in vivo.
source: Although it has been demonstrated that V1 and V2 have different substrate specificities in vivo (Goulet et al., 2007), RBM15 is the first V2-specific substrate identified.

claim: RBM15 is the first V2-specific substrate identified.
source: Although it has been demonstrated that V1 and V2 have different substrate specificities in vivo (Goulet et al., 2007), RBM15 is the first V2-specific substrate identified.
evidence: Stated as a novel finding based on the experimental data showing V2-specific dimethylation.

claim: The V2 isoform only comprises less than 5% of total PRMT1 level.
source: Of note, the V2 isoform only comprises less than 5% of total PRMT1 level, but V2 is mainly responsible for oncogenic activities in colon and breast cancers (Baldwin et al., 2012; Papadokostopoulou et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: PRMT1 V2 is mainly responsible for oncogenic activities in colon and breast cancers.
source: Of note, the V2 isoform only comprises less than 5% of total PRMT1 level, but V2 is mainly responsible for oncogenic activities in colon and breast cancers (Baldwin et al., 2012; Papadokostopoulou et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: RBM15 is involved in chromosome translocation t(1;22), which produces the fusion product RBM15-MKL1.
source: RBM15 is involved in chromosome translocation t(1;22), which produces the fusion product RBM15-MKL1 (Ma et al., 2001; Mercher et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: CNOT4 has been shown to ubiquitylate a histone demethylase Jhd2, which is responsible for erasing the histone H3K4 trimethylation marks in yeast.

claim: RBM15 interacts with histone methyltransferases complexes to maintain histone H3K4 methylation level.
source: Given that RBM15 interacts with histone methyltransferases complexes to maintain histone H3K4 methylation level (Lee and Skalnik, 2012; Xiao et al., 2015), our data provide new insights into a potential crosstalk between methyltransferases and demethylases.

source: In order to investigate the biological significance of PRMT1-mediated methylation of RBM15, we analyzed the role of PRMT1-RBM15 axis in hematopoiesis. claim: Genes such as ARHGEF1 play opposite roles at different phases of MK differentiation.
source: Genes such as ARHGEF1 (ARHGEF1,2 are in Figure 5—source data 1) play opposite roles at different phases of MK differentiation (Gao et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2012).

claim: The number of MEP progenitor cells increases, while the polypoidy of mature MKs decreases in Rbm15 knockout mice.

evidence: Based on cited literature.

source: Given that SF3B1 knockout mouse cannot mimic defects seen in myelodysplastic syndromes (Wang et al., 2014), mutations in SF3B1 are likely gain-of-function mutations.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that knockout does not recapitulate disease phenotypes.

claim: The physiological significance for multiple isoforms of c-MPL is to attenuate signaling from full-length c-MPL during MK maturation.
source: One direct consequence of RNA splicing is the altered concentration ratios between functional proteins and their alternatively spliced dominant negative counterparts. The physiological significance for multiple isoforms of c-MPL is to attenuate signaling from full-length c-MPL during MK maturation.
evidence: Inferred from the functional properties of different c-MPL isoforms.

claim: In transgenic mouse exclusively expressing full-length c-MPL, excessive production of platelets is observed.
source: In transgenic mouse exclusively expressing full-length c-MPL, excessive production of platelets is observed (Tiedt et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: Abnormal expression of GATA1s and RUNX1a are associated with leukemia.
source: Abnormal expression of GATA1s and RUNX1a are associated with leukemia (Crispino, 2005; Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: By controlling isoform ratios, HSCs fine-tune the lineage preference and the magnitude of lineage production during differentiation.
source: By controlling isoform ratios, HSCs fine-tune the lineage preference and the magnitude of lineage production during differentiation.

claim: RBM15 by binding to introns flanking the alternatively spliced exons enhances the inclusion of the exons to produce full length c-MPL mRNA.

source: In the case of GATA1, RBM15 binds to intron 1 to recruit SF3B1 to the same location (Figure 7D).

source: RBM15 facilitates the production of more full-length RUNX1b,c by skipping the exon that encodes RUNX1a.

claim: RBM15 associates with matured mRNAs.
source: Consistently, we also detected association of RBM15 with matured mRNAs (Figure 5A).

claim: RBM15 associates with transcriptional elongation factors such as Tho2 and CTR9 besides its role in transcription initiation by positively regulating histone H3K4 methylation.
source: In addition, RBM15 associates with transcriptional elongation factors such as Tho2 and CTR9 besides its role in transcription initiation by positively regulating histone H3K4 methylation (Xiao et al., 2015).

source: RBM15 has been shown to be a part of RBM20-mediated RNA splicing network in cardiomyocytes (Maatz et al., 2014; Raffel et al., 2009).

source: Thus, RBM15 is involved in the development of other tissues in addition to hematopoiesis.

claim: Splicing factors can be involved in alternative RNA polyadenylation and RNA export.
source: Given that splicing factors can be involved in alternative RNA polyadenylation and RNA export, it is not surprising that RBM15 binds to 3'UTRs for alternative RNA polyadenylation, export as well as for RNA splicing (Castelo-Branco et al., 2004; Kyburz et al., 2006).

source: Analysis by the MISO program indicates that RBM15 regulates alternative RNA splicing of genes such as HK1 by binding to 3'UTR.

claim: Both RBM15 and PRMT1 are evolutionarily conserved proteins from plants to mammals.

claim: Targeting PRMT1 may be a curative therapy to restore megakaryocyte differentiation for acute megakaryocytic leukemia.
